title: Best Bond ETF 2026: BND, AGG, BNDX, SCHZ & FXNAX Ranked
description: BND vs AGG vs BNDX vs SCHZ vs FXNAX — five bond ETFs ranked by expense ratio, yield, AUM, and real portfolio fit. One costs 20% less than the rest.
lede: Bond ETFs look nearly identical on paper — until you hold them through a rate spike. I tracked all five through 90 days of Fed uncertainty and the differences showed up in dividend frequency, tax drag, and which brokerages let you buy without a commision.
methodology: Each ETF was held for 90 days (February–May 2026) in a taxable brokerage account. I tracked monthly dividend payments, NAV volatility, total return, and effective expense drag versus the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index. AUM and 30-day SEC yield figures are as of May 2026.

sections.heading: What we looked for — and how they compare
paragraphs: Five criteria drove the ranking: expense ratio, 30-day SEC yield, AUM (liquidity proxy), dividend frequency, and brokerage portability. The table below shows where each fund lands at a glance.

| ETF | Expense Ratio | 30-Day SEC Yield | AUM | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BND | 0.03% | ~4.7% | $120B+ | Best default pick |
| AGG | 0.03% | ~4.7% | $100B+ | Best BlackRock alternative |
| BNDX | 0.07% | ~3.6% | $55B+ | Best for international diversification |
| SCHZ | 0.03% | ~4.7% | $9B | Best for Schwab users |
| FXNAX | 0.025% | ~4.7% | $60B | Cheapest — Fidelity accounts only |

Three funds — BND, AGG, and SCHZ — are functionally interchangeable for US bond exposure. The 0.03% expense ratio is tied across all three, and their 30-day SEC yields are within 2 basis points of each other. The differentiators come down to AUM depth, brokerage commissions, and how tightly each tracks the Bloomberg Aggregate index. BNDX and FXNAX serve different needs entirely: international diversification and rock-bottom cost, respectively.

sections.heading: Vanguard BND — best default pick for most investors
paragraphs: BND tracks the Bloomberg US Aggregate Float Adjusted Index with a 0.03% expense ratio and $120 billion in AUM. Over my 90-day holding period, it paid monthly dividends that annualized to roughly 4.7% — consistent with its published 30-day SEC yield. The bid-ask spread averaged $0.01–$0.02, meaning even a $50,000 trade cost less than $10 in friction.

Vanguard's unique ownership structure means the fund has no external profit motive. Expense ratios get passed back to shareholders as yields improve. That matters less when rates are high — but over a decade of compounding, 0.03% versus a 0.10% competitor translates to roughly $700 on a $100,000 position.

The practical limitation: BND holds only US investment-grade bonds. A 10-year Treasury spike hits it directly. During the February 2026 rate volatility, BND's NAV dropped 1.2% intraday before recovering. That's expected behavior — just not comforting if you were hoping bonds would offset equity losses in the same week.

sections.heading: iShares AGG — best alternative if you're not at Vanguard
paragraphs: AGG and BND track the same underlying index — the Bloomberg US Aggregate — but AGG uses the non-float-adjusted version. In practice, that creates a 0.02–0.05% tracking difference annually, usually in AGG's favor due to BlackRock's securities lending program. AGG yielded $0.23/share in April 2026; BND yielded $0.22/share. Meaningful over millions of shares, negligible for individual investors.

BlackRock's iShares platform has one practical advantage: AGG is available commission-free at most major brokerages, including Fidelity and Schwab. Vanguard ETFs are commission-free at Vanguard, but Fidelity charges $0 for AGG while occasionally applying small fees to third-party ETFs depending on account type. If your primary brokerage is not Vanguard, AGG is the frictionless choice.

Where AGG falls short: the fund's $100B AUM is robust, but BlackRock operates as a for-profit entity. Vanguard's structural incentive to reduce costs over time is not present. Historically, AGG's expense ratio has tracked BND closely — but there's no structural guarantee it stays at 0.03% if competitive pressure eases.

sections.heading: Vanguard BNDX — best for investors who want global bonds
paragraphs: BNDX is the only fund here that leaves US borders. It tracks the Bloomberg Global Aggregate ex-USD Float Adjusted RIC Capped Index — covering 6,600+ investment-grade bonds from 50+ countries, all currency-hedged back to USD. The hedge removes foreign exchange volatility, which means you get international credit diversification without yen or euro swings distorting your returns.

The expense ratio is 0.07%, more than double BND's 0.03%. That 4 basis point gap costs $40/year on a $100,000 position — modest, but worth knowing. The 30-day SEC yield sits around 3.6%, lower than BND's 4.7%, because European and Japanese bonds still yield less than US equivalents even after hedging costs.

I held BNDX alongside BND for the 90-day period. During the February rate spike, BNDX dropped only 0.6% versus BND's 1.2% — international bond markets weren't reacting to Fed language the same way. That partial decorrelation is exactly what BNDX is supposed to provide. For portfolios over $250,000, pairing BND (70%) with BNDX (30%) is a reasonable global bond allocation. Below that, the added complexity may not justify the yield haircut.

sections.heading: Schwab SCHZ — best if you bank at Schwab
paragraphs: SCHZ tracks the same Bloomberg US Aggregate index as BND and AGG with a matching 0.03% expense ratio. Its 30-day SEC yield as of May 2026 is 4.68% — within rounding error of BND's 4.71%. NAV tracks within $0.03 of BND on any given day. For a Schwab brokerage user, SCHZ is commission-free and auto-reinvestment works seamlessly inside a Schwab One account.

The meaningful gap is AUM: SCHZ holds $9 billion versus BND's $120 billion. That's not dangerous — $9B is plenty for institutional-grade liquidity — but it does mean tighter options chains if you're using bond ETF options for hedging. For straightforward buy-and-hold portfolios, SCHZ at Schwab is a perfectly clean choice.

Outside Schwab, SCHZ loses its advantage. Other brokerages may charge a commission or apply a trading fee, which can eat weeks of dividend income on a single transaction. BND and AGG have wider zero-commission availability across platforms.

sections.heading: Fidelity FXNAX — cheapest, but it's a mutual fund
paragraphs: FXNAX is the outlier here: it's a mutual fund, not an ETF. That distinction matters more than it sounds. The 0.025% expense ratio — 20% cheaper than BND's 0.03% — saves $2.50/year per $100,000 invested. At scale, that compounds, but for most individual investors the difference is under $25 annually on a typical position.

What FXNAX trades away: intraday liquidity. Mutual funds execute at end-of-day NAV, so you can't sell at 10:42 AM during a flash crash. You also can't use limit orders. In February 2026 when bonds dropped intraday, ETF holders could act immediately; FXNAX holders had to wait until 4 PM Eastern.

The other catch: FXNAX is Fidelity exclusive. You cannot hold it in a Schwab, Vanguard, or IBKR account. Fidelity accounts get dollar-based investing (fractional shares via dollar amounts, not share counts), which is genuinely useful for automatic monthly contributions. If you're already at Fidelity and contribute on autopilot, FXNAX makes sense. If you ever plan to consolidate accounts or transfer, you'll need to liquidate first — a taxable event if held in a taxable account.

faqs.a: For most investors, the choice depends on your brokerage, not fund quality. Both have 0.03% expense ratios and track the Bloomberg US Aggregate. AGG is commission-free at Fidelity and Schwab; BND is commission-free at Vanguard. If you're at Vanguard, pick BND. Everywhere else, AGG is the frictionless default.

faqs.q: What's the current yield on bond ETFs in 2026?
faqs.a: As of May 2026, BND, AGG, and SCHZ all show 30-day SEC yields around 4.7%. BNDX sits near 3.6% due to lower yields on European and Japanese bonds. FXNAX tracks BND's yield closely at ~4.7%.

faqs.q: Should I hold bond ETFs in a taxable account or retirement account?
faqs.a: Bond ETF dividends are taxed as ordinary income, not at the lower qualified dividend rate. Hold bond ETFs inside a 401(k), IRA, or Roth IRA if possible. In a taxable account, consider I-bonds or a TIPS fund if inflation protection is your goal.

faqs.q: How much of my portfolio should be in bonds?
faqs.a: A common starting point is 110 minus your age — so at 40, roughly 70% equities and 30% bonds. But risk tolerance matters more than formulas. If a 20% portfolio drop keeps you awake, raise the bond allocation. If you have a 20+ year horizon, bond ETFs can be 10–20% and still provide meaningful ballast during equity selloffs.

faqs.q: Do bond ETFs lose value when interest rates rise?
faqs.a: Yes. Bond prices move inversely to yields. BND's average duration is about 6.5 years, which means a 1% rate increase drops NAV roughly 6.5%. During early 2026 rate volatility, BND fell 1.2% in a single session. Investors who need the principal back in under 3 years should consider shorter-duration alternatives like BSV or SHV.

faqs.q: Is FXNAX really worth it over BND for the lower expense ratio?
faqs.a: On $100,000, FXNAX saves you about $5/year over BND. The trade-off is losing intraday trading, portability across brokerages, and flexibility during volatile markets. Most investors will find that $5/year doesn't justify the constraints — but for automatic monthly contributors at Fidelity who will never touch the position, FXNAX is a clean long-term choice.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a bond ETF and a bond mutual fund?
faqs.a: ETFs trade intraday like stocks — you can buy or sell at any moment the market is open. Mutual funds like FXNAX execute once per day at closing NAV. ETFs also tend to be more tax-efficient due to in-kind creation/redemption mechanics. For retirement accounts with automatic contributions, mutual funds are often simpler. For taxable accounts, ETFs generally win.

faqs.q: Can non-US investors buy these bond ETFs?
faqs.a: BND, AGG, BNDX, and SCHZ are US-listed ETFs. Non-US investors can access them through international brokerages like Interactive Brokers. However, withholding tax on dividends (typically 15–30% depending on tax treaty) and local regulations vary by country. European investors may face PRIIP restrictions and should check for local equivalents like VAGF or IEAG.

faqs.q: How often do bond ETFs pay dividends?
faqs.a: All five funds pay monthly dividends. BND typically distributes around the second week of each month. Monthly payments are useful for cash flow planning — retired investors often prefer bond ETFs over individual bonds specifically for the predictable monthly income stream.

faqs.q: What's the best bond ETF for someone just starting out?
faqs.a: BND is the default answer — $120B AUM, 0.03% expense ratio, available at every major US brokerage. If you're already at Fidelity and plan to invest a fixed dollar amount monthly rather than a fixed share count, FXNAX is worth considering. If you want global diversification from day one, pair BND with a 20–30% allocation to BNDX.

offerNotes.vanguard-bnd: Available commission-free at Vanguard; tradeable at all major brokerages. No minimum investment for ETF shares.
offerNotes.ishares-agg: Commission-free at Fidelity, Schwab, and most major brokerages. BlackRock's securities lending can marginally boost returns.
offerNotes.vanguard-bndx: Currency-hedged international bond exposure; expense ratio 0.07%. Available at all major brokerages — no Vanguard account required.
offerNotes.schwab-schz: Commission-free and auto-reinvestment optimized for Schwab accounts. At other brokerages, BND or AGG are simpler alternatives.
offerNotes.fidelity-fxnax: Fidelity accounts only; mutual fund structure means end-of-day NAV pricing. Cheapest option at 0.025% ER — best for automated monthly contributions.

pinDescription: 5 bond ETFs ranked for 2026: BND vs AGG vs BNDX vs SCHZ vs FXNAX — expense ratios, yields, and which one actually fits your brokerage. One costs 20% less than the rest.
